steps.title: Monitor

treatment.method_description: Select treatment methods based on disease type, severity, crop stage, and local regulations.

methods.title: Cultural Control
methods.description: Change how the crop is grown so the disease finds it harder to spread.
points: Manage water and drain the field when needed
Remove weeds and infected crop residue

methods.title: Biological Control
methods.description: Use natural organisms and products that suppress disease-causing microbes.
points: Use compost and organic matter to improve soil health
Protect natural enemies in the field
Combine with cultural control for better results

methods.title: Resistant Varieties
methods.description: Grow rice varieties that tolerate or resist diseases common in your area.
points: Ask the local agriculture office for suitable varieties
Avoid planting one variety over very large areas
Keep good seed for the next season

methods.title: Chemical Control
methods.description: Fungicides and bactericides can help when disease is serious or spreading fast.
points: Use only products approved for rice
Apply at the recommended time and rate on the label
Follow the waiting period before harvest

treatment.guide_title: What Should You Do for Different Problems?
treatment.disease_description: Open a disease to see what to do in the field.
treatment.what_to_do: What to do in the field
treatment.general_guidance: This page gives general guidance only. Disease pressure, rice variety, and local rules differ between areas. Before using any chemical product, confirm the product and dose with your local agriculture officer or the label.

blast.name: Rice Blast
cultural: Use resistant varieties and healthy seed
Avoid excess nitrogen; split fertilizer into smaller doses
Keep the field from drying out during the growing stage
Remove and destroy infected straw after harvest
blast.chemical: If leaf lesions spread quickly or the neck is at risk, ask your local agriculture office about a fungicide approved for rice, and apply it at the recommended stage.

bacterial_blight.name: Bacterial Leaf Blight
cultural: Plant certified seed and resistant varieties
Avoid cutting or damaging leaf tips when transplanting
Drain the field to reduce spread after heavy rain or flooding
Avoid excess nitrogen and keep field edges free of weeds
bacterial_blight.chemical: Fungicides do not control bacteria. Rely on resistant varieties and field hygiene, and ask the agriculture office before using any bactericide.

brown_spot.name: Brown Spot
cultural: Correct poor soil with balanced fertilizer, including potassium
Avoid water stress and drought during growth
brown_spot.chemical: Brown spot is usually linked to weak crop nutrition. Improve the soil first, and use a fungicide only for a severe outbreak on the advice of an agriculture officer.

sheath_blight.name: Sheath Blight
cultural: Do not plant too densely; give plants room and airflow
Remove weeds and crop residue that carry the fungus
Drain the field to lower humidity at the base of the plants
sheath_blight.chemical: Treat early, when lesions first appear on lower leaf sheaths. Use a rice-approved fungicide as advised locally and follow the label.

treatment.safety_title: Protect Your Family, Crop, and Environment
treatment.safety_description: Good safety habits keep farmers healthy and prevent harm to water, fish, and nearby crops.
safety_items: Wear gloves, a mask, long sleeves, and boots when spraying
Read and follow the product label every time
Never spray in strong wind or just before rain
Keep chemicals away from canals, ponds, and drinking water
Store products in their original container, away from children
Wash your hands and clothes after spraying
treatment.cta_title: Not Sure Which Disease Your Rice Has?
treatment.cta_description: Identify the disease first. Use our Expert System to match your field symptoms and get a diagnosis with prevention advice.
treatment.understanding: Understanding rice disease treatment helps farmers choose timely actions and avoid unnecessary or harmful practices.
treatment.important_note: Always follow local agricultural guidance and product labels. If you are uncertain about a diagnosis or treatment, consult an agricultural expert.
